title: Ali 'Imran
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Āl ʿImrān is the third surah of the Qur'an, and the longest after al-Baqarah. It has two hundred verses, it was revealed in Madinah, and it carries a family name rather than the name of a place or a thing. Its subject is the one God and the straight path. It opens with the Oneness of Allah and with the Book, spends much of its middle on the People of the Book and on the family of Maryam, and closes with the life of the first community, its laws, its battles and its manners.

### What the name means

Āl ʿImrān means "the family of ʿImrān". The name is not imported from outside the surah, because its own opening verses use it. They describe the Torah as sent down to Mūsā (Moses) son of ʿImrān, and the second verse names Allah as al-Hayyul al-Qayyūm, the Ever Living, the One who sustains and protects all that exists. Later the surah turns to the family of Maryam (Mary) and to the son she bore, ʿĪsā (Jesus), and gives them several sections of their own.

### When it was revealed

Āl ʿImrān was revealed in Madinah, and the evidence for that sits in the opening run of the surah itself. Its first eighty-three ayat all belong to the story of a delegation that came from Najran to Madinah in the ninth year of the Hijrah (632 CE). The account of that meeting, and the verse about the mubahalah (3:61), belong to the same run. The virtues of Āl ʿImrān were set out together with the virtues of al-Baqarah, at the head of the long surah that comes before this one.

### How it connects to the surah before it

Al-Fatihah ends with a prayer for guidance to the straight path. Al-Baqarah then opens with the words "This Book which has no doubt in it", and that opening is read as the answer to the prayer. The Book has been sent down, and it is guidance. From there al-Baqarah gives many of the injunctions of the Islamic law, speaks often of the hostility of the disbelievers and of the need to confront them, and ends in the voice of prayer with the words "Help us, then, against disbelieving people".

Āl ʿImrān takes that plea up and works it out. The surah deals with the ways believers are to deal with disbelievers, and with the need to carry out jihad against them, verbally and physically. In that sense it is an elaboration and an extension of the last line of the surah before it.

### The Oneness of Allah in the opening verses

The first five verses of the surah set out tawhid, the Oneness of Allah. This is the basic point of difference between Islam and other religions, and between a disbeliever and a true Muslim. Those who believe in the Oneness of Allah and in all His prophets are Muslims, and those who do not are disbelievers.

The surah then argues for that truth out of the history of the prophets. Adam was the first to carry the message of the Oneness of Allah before human beings, and his descendants kept it until their ways drifted from the original message. After a long stretch of time Nuh (Noah) called people back to the same principle. Later Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), Isḥāq (Isaac) and Yaʿqūb (Jacob), born in Iraq and Syria, rose with the same call. Then came Mūsā (Moses), Hārūn (Aaron) and other prophets in that order, all holding to the same principle and inviting people to it. After another long stretch of time ʿĪsā (Jesus) rose with the same call. In the end Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ came with the common call of all the prophets.

The argument rests on the size of the agreement. Some one hundred and twenty four thousand blessed prophets were born in different periods, speaking different languages and living in different countries. Writing was not in vogue in their age, so a prophet could not have reached another one's writings, and most of them never met in person. They appeared centuries apart, and each had no source of information about the others except the revelation received from Allah alone. The agreement of so large a body of people, spread across so many times and places, may be enough to establish the principle in itself, even without looking at their personal qualities. When one does look at them, at the highest possible standards of truth and justice they held, there is more reason still to believe that their message was true and their call was sound.

A hadith carries the same point in a shorter form. Some Christians came to the Prophet ﷺ and spoke with him about religion. He set these two verses before them as arguments confirming the Oneness of Allah, and they had no answer with which to refute them.

### The Book, and the criterion

The Creator and Sustainer of the universe is not a mechanical God. He is a living and conscious Being, and He has sent guidance to people throughout the ages, including the Torah and the Bible, revealed to the prophets before. People have always put their own constructions on divine teaching, and through their own self-styled interpretations they have split one religion into many. In the end the final Book was sent down to people, the Qur'an. It is a genuine book of guidance, and at the same time it is the criterion, the standard that shows which is the true religion and which is the religion people have devised for themselves.

Those who deny the Book of the Almighty and refuse to give up the religion they have invented deserve punishment. They are the people to whom eyes were granted, and they did not see the light. They are the people to whom minds were granted, and they did not understand the truth when it came to them as argument. Bending to the truth meant bowing to the Prophet and to Allah, and they thought that surrendering to the Supreme Being and to His Prophet would make them smaller. To keep their own petty greatness, they refused to bow to the truth.

### What the surah covers

The surah's own outline, from beginning to end, runs in this order. It opens with the divine opening and the supreme Oneness of Allah, then with Allah's complete knowledge and creative power, and with the nature of the Qur'anic verses, some of them clear and some of them allegorical. It moves on to the fate of the disbelievers and to lessons taken from history, to divine support at the battle of Badr, to the deception of worldly pleasures, to the everlasting rewards for the righteous, to the declaration of one God and one true religion, and to the punishment of those who killed prophets and refused justice.

It then turns to the self-deception of those who reject divine judgment, to the sovereignty of Allah over all things, to the command not to take disbelievers as allies over believers, and to the path of Allah's love, which is to follow the Prophet ﷺ. From there it reaches the chosen families in human history, the story of Maryam's mother and her dedication, the story of Zakariyya and the birth of Yahya (John), the honour of Maryam above all women, the miraculous birth of ʿĪsā, and the mission and miracles that followed. It describes the disciples of ʿĪsā, the plot against him and Allah's protection of him, the reward of believers and disbelievers, and the likeness of ʿĪsā to Adam, which answers the claim that he was divine.

The last part of the surah is about the community that receives the Book. It holds the challenge to settle the disputes about ʿĪsā, the call to common ground in pure monotheism, the truth about Ibrāhīm, the deceptions of some of the People of the Book, the covenant between Allah and His prophets, the unity of the believers and holding fast to Allah, the differing fates of the two groups on the Day of Judgment, the excellence and the responsibility of the Muslim nation, the lessons of Badr and Uhud, the law of the community with its ban on usury, the qualities of the righteous, the martyrs, and the closing advice about the life to come.

### In short

- Two hundred verses, revealed in Madinah, and named for a family rather than a place.
- It continues the prayer of al-Fatihah and the answer that al-Baqarah began, and it works out the "Help us against disbelieving people" that closed the earlier surah.
- Its first teaching is tawhid, the Oneness of Allah, argued from the one message carried by every prophet from Adam to Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ.
- Its middle follows the People of the Book and the story of Maryam, Zakariyya, Yahya and ʿĪsā, and its close turns to the laws, unity, battles and manners of the first community.

1.text:
The surah opens with three letters and nothing else, "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm". What they mean is known best to Allah, and the verses that follow them work out what they point to. The second verse names Allah alone as worthy of worship, the third announces the Book sent down to the Prophet ﷺ, and the fourth warns of the punishment that waits for those who reject the signs of Allah. The letters are a threshold, and what stands behind them is the first statement of the surah's subject and the first argument for it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Alif-Lãm-Mĩm"**: three letters, and the first thing a reader meets in this surah. The same three letters open al-Baqarah, and their placement was dealt with there. One view is that they expose how weak the Arabs were. They had the same letters that make up their own speech, and still they could not bring a Qur'an like this one. Another view is simply that Allah knows best what He means by these letters. The surah does not explain them here, and the detail of such words of hidden meaning is given later in the section.

### What each letter alludes to

**The Alif** alludes to the way Allah is enough for you, in every situation you are in. People are held by carelessness and have not lost the road of right action and right thinking. Allah is the One who starts in motion whatever puts you back on the road, and no one else is enough for you in what helps you there. He does not wait for you to ask. Even if you have no idea what state you are in, and even if you do not perceive it, His sufficiency is already there. And He gives without your seeking.

**The Lām** alludes to the kindness, luṭf, that Allah shows you at the finest and most hidden level, so fine that you cannot see the spot where His favor strengthens you.

**The Mīm** alludes to how the stream of divine determination, taqdīr, fits in with the circumstances the friends of Allah ask for. Nothing stirs in this world, and nothing shows itself, unless it brings good pleasure to them. Going too far is not the issue when we say that in His words "Every day He is upon some matter" (55:29), what the matter is, is the coming about of what the friends desire.

### Why the surah begins with letters that carry no meaning on their own

These disconnected letters run against the ordinary customs of human speech. It is said that by listening to them every concept disappears from the hearts, whether a known written custom or something the mind has invented, and whether the concept comes out of necessity, Ḍarūra, out of sensory perception, ḥiss, or out of independent reasoning, ijtihād. Once hearts are emptied in that way, and innermost selves are purified of what is familiar and customary, the name Allah reaches a heart that is sanctified from everything besides Him, and an innermost self that is clean of every mode of inquiry, kayf.

### A report from Ibn ʿAbbās

Ibn ʿAbbās said that Allah told them of the coming of the delegation of Najran. The letters have also been read as an oath, in which Allah swears that He is One and has neither child nor partner.

### The Greatest Name in this verse and in 2:255

A hadith says that the Greatest Name of Allah is contained in two verses, the verse of Ayat Al-Kursi (2:255) and this opening of the surah, "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists" (3:1-2). The letters themselves were explained at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and the meaning of al-Hayyul al-Qayyūm was explained at the verse of Ayat Al-Kursi.

### In short

- Three letters open the surah, and their meaning is left with Allah.
- They show the limits of human speech, since the same letters make up ordinary words and cannot make a Qur'an.
- Each letter points to a different aspect of Allah: His sufficiency, His kindness and His ordering of events.
- A hadith places the Greatest Name of Allah in this opening and in the verse of Ayat Al-Kursi (2:255).

2.text:
The second verse states the Oneness of Allah in plain words: "Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining". It is the first full statement of the surah's subject, and it works in two moves. It declares, and then it argues, because the two names that follow the declaration are the argument.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah!"**: the name itself opens the verse, and a statement of the Oneness has to begin there.

**"There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him"**: here the Oneness of Allah is stated as a categorical declaration. The sense of it is that nothing at all is worthy of worship apart from Allah. In the terms of Islamic theology, the letters that came before gave a rational proof, and this verse gives a reported proof. A rational proof rests on argument. A reported proof rests on a verse of a divine book, on a declaration made by an authority, or on a report narrated by a trustworthy person.

**"the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining"**: al-Hayyul al-Qayyūm. The first is the One who never dies and is not evanescent. The second is the Self-subsistent who has no beginning. These two names carry the rational proof of the verse.

### What worship demands of the one who is worshipped

To worship someone is to stand before that person in complete submission and humility. So the one who is worshipped has to stand at the top of honour and power, and has to be perfect in every respect.

The conclusion is plain. A thing that cannot hold its own being, and has to depend on somebody else even to exist, can hardly claim honour or power of its own.

### Nothing that depends on another can be worshipped

Everything else in this world is ruled out by the same test. Be it an idol carved out of stone, or water, or a tree, or an angel, or an apostle, a thing that cannot start itself and cannot hold itself together is in no condition to be worshipped. Only the One who was alive before everything, who is present now, and who will go on living and sustaining, can be worshipped. That Being can only be Allah. Nobody else is worthy of worship.

### The Ever-Living is the one who never takes His eyes off you

Allah alone is worthy of worship. He lives perfectly, without any death or deficiency, and He exists by Himself, so He is not in need of any of His creation. The creation exists only through Him and is always in need of Him. He does not get drawn away so that He becomes too busy for you, and He does not fail to attend so that you are left with nothing. He watches, raqīb, over the deepest states of your inner self. Alone or among people, His watchfulness is the same, and in whatever condition you find yourself, He is your Beloved, ḥabīb.

### The words of hidden meaning

The Alif Lam Mim at the head of the first verse belongs to a special set of words used by the Qur'an, words of hidden meaning known as mutashabihāt. The true meaning of these is kept between Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and the section clears it up a little further on. The answer to the doubts that disbelievers nurse comes at the end of this section, where the verse turns to what is hidden from sight and to the shaping of every person in the womb.

### In short

- The verse declares that nothing is worthy of worship except Allah, and then argues the point from two of His names.
- Worship requires perfection, and nothing that depends on another being can be perfect in the way worship requires.
- Idols, water, trees, angels and apostles are all ruled out by that test.
- Allah is the Ever-Living and All-Sustaining, and He watches the believer in every state.

3.text:
The third verse turns from the name of Allah to His sending down a Book: "He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth, confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel". The point of the verse is that the Book is not a new claim. It arrives with the truth, and it confirms what was sent down before it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth"**: the Book was sent down with truth, which means there is no doubt or suspicion that it comes from Allah. Allah revealed it with His knowledge, and the angels testify to that fact, and Allah is sufficient as a witness. The Book was sent to you, Muhammad ﷺ, and Gabriel was sent with it, so that truth might be shown apart from falsehood.

**"confirming what came before it"**: this means the previous Books, sent down to the servants and prophets of Allah. Those Books testify to the truth of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an in turn bears witness to what they held, among them the glad tidings of Muhammad's prophethood and of the descent of the Glorious Qur'an. Even though the books were sent to the messengers before you, the remembrance, dhikr, of you was not left out of any of them. The one who spoke for them said that the pages of their absent beloveds carry his name on their title page, and just as the lights of the prophets were extended through you, everything revealed was adorned with the remembrance of you. Briefly put, one can say that the Oneness of Allah is not peculiar to the Qur'an or to the Prophet of Islam. Long before, Allah sent down Books such as the Torah and the Injil, and sent prophets of His own, and every one of them taught this and carried it as the message of his mission. When the Qur'an came, it simply confirmed their truth. It put forward no new claim that anyone had to struggle to understand or accept.

**"as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel"**: the Torah was sent to Mūsā (Moses) son of ʿImrān, and the Injil to ʿĪsā (Jesus) son of Mary, before the Qur'an was revealed. Whenever the Qur'an speaks of the Torah and the Injil it means the original books revealed to Moses and Jesus, so these words should not be confused with the Old and New Testaments of today. The Qur'an itself was revealed in instalments, with true stories and just laws that agree with the earlier books, and there is no contradiction between them all.

### In short

- The Book was sent down with truth, and Allah's knowledge and the angels' testimony stand behind it.
- It confirms the earlier Books, and they in turn confirm it, including the glad tidings of the Prophet ﷺ.
- The Torah went to Mūsā son of ʿImrān and the Injil to ʿĪsā son of Mary, and the Qur'an adds no new claim.

4.text:
The fourth verse finishes the account of the Books: "previously, as a guide for people, and ˹also˺ revealed the Standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺. Surely those who reject Allah’s revelations will suffer a severe torment. For Allah is Almighty, capable of punishment". The first half describes what the earlier Books did and what the last Book does. The second half warns.

### Phrase by phrase

**"previously, as a guide for people"**: before the Qur'an, and before Muhammad ﷺ, the Torah and the Gospel were sent down as guidance for people, guiding the Children of Israel from error and leading those who followed these two Books in their own time. The word used for the sending down of the Torah and the Injil is different from the one used for the Qur'an, and the reason given is that the Qur'an comes in instalments, while the two Books were revealed in one go.

**"and ˹also˺ revealed the Standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺"**: the criterion, al-furqān, tells misguidance, falsehood and deviation apart from guidance, truth and piety. It is the standard that separates the lawful from the unlawful, and it works through the signs, plain evidences and clear proofs it contains and through its explanations. It is mentioned after the three Scriptures so that it embraces all revealed Scripture besides them. All these books held guidance and directed people to the best of this world and the afterlife.

**"Surely those who reject Allah’s revelations will suffer a severe torment. For Allah is Almighty, capable of punishment"**: those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah denied and refused them, and for them is a severe torment on the Day of Resurrection. Their chastisement is the ignominy of the veil, though they do not perceive it. Allah is Mighty, victorious in His affair, so that nothing can stop Him from carrying out His promise and His threat. He is Lord of Retribution with a severe punishment for those who disobey Him, the like of which none can do. Everyone seeks what is precious, but most do not find it, and Allah is Precious, ʿazīz, to His friends and Lord of Retribution to His enemies.

### The Oneness of Allah is confirmed by what these verses say of Him

The last part of this section strengthens the doctrine of the Oneness on the ground of two attributes. Encompassing knowledge and unlimited power are strong proofs of the One who possesses eternal, all-encompassing knowledge, and whose power controls everything. Anyone with imperfect knowledge and limited power cannot be entrusted with this exalted station. The signs of Allah referred to here, and the doom that follows rejecting them, are aimed in this context at the delegation of Najran, and the doom is heavy both in this world and in the next.

### In short

- The Torah and the Gospel came before, as guidance, and the Qur'an came in instalments as the criterion.
- The criterion separates truth from falsehood, and it embraces all revealed Scripture.
- Rejecting the signs of Allah brings a severe torment, and Allah is Mighty and able to punish.

5.text:
The fifth verse is short and wide: "Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah". After the Book and its warnings, the surah turns to the One who sent them down, and describes Him as the one whose knowledge has no gaps at all.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah"**: nothing in the earth or in the heavens is hidden from His watch. He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and the earth. In this context the earth holds the story of the delegation of Najran, and the heavens hold the business of the angels, and neither is hidden from Him. He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. Nothing, no existent thing at all, is hidden in heaven and earth from Allah, because of His knowledge of universals and particulars. Heaven and earth are named here because the senses of people do not reach beyond them.

### Every breath is counted

A servant does not breathe a single breath without Allah counting it, muḥṣīh. No particle is found in the heaven or the earth unless He brought it into being and sustains it, mubdiʿ. And no quality or attribute belongs to anyone unless He is the governor of it, mutawallī. That is the level of ordinary people, ʿumūm. The elect, khuṣūṣ, stand higher: nobody puts a need to Him without His meeting it, qāḌīhā, and nobody meets a calamity without His sufficing for it, kāfīhā.

### Why only Allah can give guidance

Only Allah can tell us the truth about Himself, about His being and about His attributes, and He has set that out plainly in His Book, so that a reader who is keen to know Him finds real light there. Only He can guide anyone. The right course for a person can be settled by no one but the One who has known people from their birth to their death, and who knows what went before the birth and what lies beyond the death. So it is Allah alone who can set the nature of people inside the whole universe and decree the kind of conduct that will secure their success in this world and the next, since a sound human mind can only be one in step with the rest of the world and in accord with the larger order of the cosmos. And it is Allah alone who has both the knowledge and the power to say what people should be aiming at in the present world. On that basis, the only sensible thing for a person to do is to trust in the Maker and to take His guidance whole, with complete confidence.

### In short

- Nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah, and He knows universals and particulars.
- Every breath is counted, every particle is created by Him, and every need is met by Him.
- Only He can settle the right course of people, because only He knows the whole of their life and the whole of the universe.

6.text:
The sixth verse closes the opening section: "He is the One Who shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—the Almighty, All-Wise". The verse does two things at once. It names Allah as the one who forms every human being, and it rules out every other claimant to worship.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills"**: He forms you in the wombs however He wishes, a man or a woman, attractive or otherwise, happy or unhappy, short or tall, fair or ugly, blessed or doomed, white or black or anything else. It is by His supreme wisdom that billions of men and women have been given clear and distinguishable features, so that each one is a person distinct from all the others.

**"There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him"**: He is the Creator, and so He is the only deity worthy of worship, without partners. His is the perfect might, wisdom and decision, and no one else has any of it. Nobody else deserves the love and reverence of worship. He is Mighty in His kingdom and cannot be overpowered, and He is Wise in His planning and legislation.

### Why this verse answers the claim that ʿĪsā is divine

One can say that the verse settles the question of ʿĪsā, the son of Mary. He is a servant, created, like everybody else that Allah creates. Allah made him in his mother's womb and shaped him as He willed, and his creation moved from one stage to the next, as Allah said, "He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation in three veils of darkness" (39:6). So on what ground could ʿĪsā be a god, as the Christians claim?

### The reports on the form of the Creator

In a sound report MuṣṬafā said, "God created Adam in His form, and his height was sixty cubits". It has also been narrated as "in the form of His face". Some who follow interpretation turned the referent of the pronoun away from Allah and rejected the outward sense, on the ground that their religion rests on interpretation and denial of the outward meaning. Those who follow the sunnah, whose way is to hear, to accept and to surrender, leave interpretation aside and keep the outward sense. Their view is that the pronoun in that report points to Allah, that no investigation or interpretation is allowed here, and that imagining a likeness is a mistake, since Allah has no equal in any of His attributes. On the question of vision, many reports describe the Real as having a shining face and form. Ibn ʿAbbās narrates that MuṣṬafā said, "I saw my Lord in the most beautiful form." In the narrative of Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī, MuṣṬafā said, "My Lord was shown to me in the most beautiful form. He said, 'O Muḥammad!' I said, 'Here I am, obeying Thee.' About what are the Higher Plenum disputing?" The narrative of Jābir ibn Samura is this: "Surely God disclosed Himself to me in the most beautiful form." The narrative of Anas is this: "My Lord came to me in the most beautiful form." Anas also said that among the favors Allah will grant Adam on the Day of Resurrection is this: He will say, "Did I not bestow upon you My form?" Ibn ʿAbbās said that Moses was angry with the Children of Israel, and when he came down with a prohibition he told them, "Drink this, you donkeys!" Allah asked him whether creatures made in His own form could be likened to donkeys. It is well known, the reports of the resurrection say, that MuṣṬafā said, "God will come to them in other than the form in which they recognize Him."

### In short

- Allah shapes every person in the womb as He wills, and no one else has that power.
- That is why ʿĪsā is a created servant like the rest of us, and cannot be a god.
- The reports on the form of the Creator are read, by those who follow the sunnah, as referring to Allah, with no likeness imagined.

7.text:
This verse, "He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book, of which some verses are precise—they are the foundation of the Book—while others are elusive", gives a rule for reading the whole Qur'an. Some verses settle meaning, and some do not. The clear ones form "the foundation of the Book", and the elusive ones must be read under their control. The verse then divides readers by how they handle that difference, and it closes with the answer of "those well-grounded in knowledge, they say, “We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord.”"

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book"**: Allah sent Gabriel with the Scripture to Muhammad ﷺ. The verse begins with the sending down because the dispute that follows is a dispute about how the Book is to be read.

**"of which some verses are precise"**: these are the muḥkam verses, entirely clear and plain, and they are the basis of the Qur'an. They state what is allowed and what is forbidden, the laws, limits, obligations and rulings that must be believed in and put into practice. They are clear to anyone who knows the rules of Arabic grammar well, and most of the Book belongs to this kind.

**"they are the foundation of the Book"**: they are called Umm al-Kitāb, mother of the Book, because they are the root and essence of all its teaching. Whoever refers the unclear verses to them reaches correct guidance, and whoever does the opposite goes astray. When people disagree, they are the reference point.

**"while others are elusive"**: these are the mutāshabih verses, which carry more than one possible meaning. Some of their meanings agree with the clear verses, and some carry literal signals that are not the intended sense. Abrogated verses, parables, oaths, and things that must be believed but not put into practice also fall into this kind.

**"Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking ˹to spread˺ doubt through their ˹false˺ interpretations"**: people misguided and turned from truth to falsehood pick out the unclear verses because their wording covers such a wide area that it can be bent to serve a false reading. The clear verses cannot be bent, so they stand as unequivocal proof against such people. Seeking doubt, al-fitnah, means seeking to misguide followers by pretending to prove an innovation from the Qur'an, so the conduct is marked as dangerous by the Prophet's own warning, given in the hadith that follows.

**"but none grasps their ˹full˺ meaning except Allah"**: the word used here is taʾwīl. What taʾwīl means, and where the sentence should pause, is taken up in the section below on the pause in this phrase.

**"As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say, “We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord.”"**: the grounded believe in both kinds. Both the clear and the elusive are true, and each testifies to the other, because both come from Allah and nothing that comes from Allah contains contradiction. Allah states the test Himself: "Do they not then consider the Qur'an carefully? Had it been from other than Allah, they would surely have found therein many a contradiction" (4:82).

**"But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason"**: only those with good minds and sound comprehension take admonition here. The word translated as being mindful is yadhdhakkar, in which an initial tāʾ has been assimilated into the dhāl, and the people named are those with pith, the possessors of intellect.

### Why this verse came down when it did

The first five verses of the surah set out the Oneness of Allah, and the text now answers doubts raised against it. A group of Christians came to the Prophet ﷺ and discussed religion with him. He refuted their doctrine of the Trinity in detail and proved the Oneness of Allah from His eternal existence, perfect power, all-encompassing knowledge and unique creative act, and it was agreed that once the Oneness stood, the Trinity could not stand with it.

The Christians then turned to the Qur'an itself. ʿĪsā (Jesus) is called in it Rūḥullāh, the Spirit of Allah, and Kalimatullāh, the Word of Allah. In their reading, those titles gave him a share in divinity. This verse settles that question. Titles of that kind belong to the elusive verses, so they cannot be read against the clear ones, and the clear ones speak plainly. "He ['Isa] was not more than a servant. We granted Our favor to him" (43:59). And, "Verily, the likeness of 'Isa before Allah is the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then (He) said to him: 'Be!' and he was" (3:59). Anyone who shuts his eyes to those verses and pulls at the elusive titles until they yield a godhood that the clear verses deny is simply going astray and being obstinate.

### Two kinds of verse, in plain terms

There are two kinds of subject in the Qur'an, and the style follows the subject. Some things belong to the known human world, such as historical events, signs in the universe and commandments for this life. They are put in a direct style, and they can be understood precisely. Other things belong to the unseen matters that no one can grasp in this life, such as the attributes of Allah and the states of Heaven and Hell. Everyday language cannot carry them, so they are framed in an allegorical style. If one says "man's hand", that is a plain statement of fact. If one says "God's hand", that is an allegory. A reader who misses this falls into taking allegorical verses literally, which leads away from the truth and never arrives at it.

Muḥammad ibn Ishaq bin Yasar described the clear verses as carrying the Lord's proof, protecting servants, and answering opponents and falsehood. Their intended sense is fixed. The unclear verses, he said, admit tampering with words even though tampering is forbidden. Allah tests servants through them just as He tests them through what is permitted and what is banned, so no one may twist them toward a false sense.

Another way of putting the difference is to say that the clear verses are rules that are acted upon and not abrogated, and that they are the leading theme in every Book. The example given is "Say: Come, I will recite unto you that which your Lord hath made a sacred duty for you" (6:151). The elusive verses are then described in two ways. In one, they are vague in meaning, like the letters of the alphabet used by their numerical value, ḥisāb al-Jumal, in Alif Lām Mīm and the other openings of surahs. In the other, they are the verses that were abrogated and are no longer acted upon. The whole Qur'an can also be called clear in one sense and allegorical in another. It is called clear where Allah says, "A Book whose verses have been made clear", meaning that it contains no imperfections. And it is called allegorical where Allah says, "A Book consimilar", meaning that its parts resemble each other in beauty and veracity.

### Who pursues the elusive verses, and what they want

The deviating pictured here were given names. Kaʿb Ibn al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab are named, men whose hearts held scepticism, opposition and turning away from guidance. They pursued the allegorical part of the Qur'an in order to hold fast to unbelief, to ascribe partners to Allah, and to keep their own error, and they did so by trying to work out the future of this community from it, hoping that dominion would come back to them. Allah's answer is that the explanation of that belongs to Him alone, and at that point He interrupts His own speech and begins again with the grounded in knowledge. Those of sound instruction, who have a sound grasp of the Torah, are then described as ʿAbdullāh Ibn Salām and his companions, sound-minded men who accept the simile of the Qur'an and say that both kinds of verse are from their Lord.

The warning was given in a hadith too. Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿĀʾishah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this verse and then said, "When you see those who argue in it, using the parts that are not clear, then they are those whom Allah meant. Therefore, beware of them." Al-Bukhārī recorded a similar hadith from ʿĀʾishah in his explanation of this verse, Muslim recorded it in his book on the Divine Will in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and Abū Dāwūd recorded it in the section on the Sunnah in his Sunan, with the wording, "When you see those who follow what is not so clear of the Qur'an, then they are those whom Allah described, so beware of them." ʿĀʾishah is also quoted in more modest words: when people are seen busy investigating the elusive verses, they should be kept at a distance, because they are the same people Allah has talked about.

A second hadith names three fears for the community, the ummah. The first is that people grow wealthy and begin to envy one another, and that envy opens rifts and bloodshed. The second is that the Book of Allah is trifled with, with even the uninitiated and the ignorant claiming a perfect understanding through translations, and with the very things that are not meant to be understood becoming the great object of study, although Allah alone knows their meaning. The third is that people let their knowledge go to waste once it has grown, by stopping the work of increasing it.

### Where the sentence pauses, and what taʾwīl means

Scholars of Qur'an recitation differ over where to pause in the words "none knows its taʾwīl except Allah", and the differing answers depend on what taʾwīl means. The pause after the name of Allah was reported from ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah, Abū ash-Shaʿthāʾ and Abū Nahīk. Others pause after "those who are firmly grounded in knowledge" and make them sharers in the knowing, arguing that the Qur'an does not address people with what they cannot understand at all. Ibn ʿAbbās was quoted by Mujāhid, through Ibn Abī Najīḥ, as saying, "I am among those who are firmly grounded in its taʾwīl." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed for Ibn ʿAbbās in these words: "O Allah! Bestow on him knowledge in the religion and teach him the Ta'wil (interpretation)."

Taʾwīl has two meanings in the Qur'an. In the first, it is the true reality of a thing and what it will turn out to be. That is the sense in Yūsuf's words, "O my father! This is the Ta'wil of my dream aforetime!" (12:100). And it is the sense in the waiting for the reality of the Resurrection in "Await they just for its Ta'wil?" (7:53), where the reality they were told about is what is awaited. With that meaning, the pause must come after the name of Allah, because only Allah knows the true reality of things, and "those who are firmly grounded in knowledge" then begin a new sentence describing their conduct.

In the second, taʾwīl means explanation and description. That is the sense in "Inform us of the Ta'wil of this" (12:36), where people ask for an explanation. With that meaning, the pause comes after "those who are firmly grounded in knowledge", because the learned do have general knowledge of what they were addressed with and can understand it, even though they do not know the true reality of things. The verse about the coming of the Lord is explained on the same footing: "And your Lord comes, and the angels, in rows" (89:22) means that your Lord will come and the angels will come in ranks, and that much can be stated without claiming to know the reality of it. Ibn Jarīr transmitted part of this discussion in his reports on the verse.

### Who the grounded in knowledge are

Nāfiʿ bin Yazīd said, in a report recorded by Ibn al-Mundhir, that those firmly grounded in knowledge are the people who are modest for the sake of Allah, seek His pleasure with humility, and neither exaggerate the standing of those above them nor belittle those below them. The weightier description given is that they are the main body of Muslims, ahl al-sunnah wa'l-jamāʿah, who accept only the interpretation of the Qur'an and the Sunnah that has been authentically reported from the Companions and the righteous generations after them and that carries the agreement of the community. They hold that the clear verses are the axis and centre of the Qur'an. What lies beyond their understanding in the elusive verses they leave with Allah, confessing the limits of their knowledge and insight. They are never proud of their knowledge, however complete it may seem, and never proud of the strength of their faith. Instead they pray constantly for steadfastness, grace and mercy. They have no appetite for mischief, so they do not make the elusive verses the object of their intellectual pursuit. The clear verses they needed for life, and those meanings Allah did not keep secret. The elusive ones He chose not to disclose, so believing in them as they stand is enough.

### The inner reading of the opening words

There is also an inward reading of the verse, and it begins with a single word, Huwa, "He". The word points to being itself rather than naming or describing. It declares that our Lord exists, rightly exists, and has always existed, without place and raised above attributes. Shurayḥ ʿĀbid recalled a dervish praying inside the Sanctuary mosque: "O He who is He! Beside You there is no he. Forgive me." From the Unseen came an answer that angels would keep writing the reward of the first utterance until resurrection.

The letters teach return. The ḥ comes from the throat's far end while the w begins at its near opening, suggesting that speech starts with Him and finally comes back to Him. Created beings follow the same arc, issued by His power at the beginning and recalled by His decree at the end. A rapt dervish answered every inquiry (name, origin, desire) with "He". When the others suggested that God was meant, he heard that name and surrendered his spirit, leaving the world. People picture Your name in a hundred senses, surrender their lives while remembering it, and pour out life for the fragrance of union while possessing only incapacity to describe You.

The two divisions then mirror two faces of religion: outward law's majesty in clear texts, and inner reality's beauty in difficult texts. Common people need the outward side first, perceiving and practising toward blessings and joy.

Ibn ʿAbbās set the same boundary in a shorter form. Explanation is of four types: explanation that the Arabs know from their language, explanation that no one is excused for not knowing, explanation that the scholars know, and explanation that only Allah knows. The elusive verses are left open by that fourth type, and the answer of the grounded is belief first, and then the supplication of the next two verses.

### In short

- The Qur'an has clear verses, the root of all its teaching, and elusive verses that must be read under their control.
- People with deviating hearts chase the elusive verses to spread doubt, often to defend error or to claim knowledge of the future, and the Prophet ﷺ warned against them by name and description.
- Only Allah knows the true reality of the elusive verses, though the learned can explain what can be explained. The grounded believe in both kinds, because all of it is from their Lord.

8.text:
The eighth verse gives the prayer of the people described in the verse before it: "˹They say,˺ “Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us. Grant us Your mercy. You are indeed the Giver ˹of all bounties˺.”" Men and women of real knowledge do not trust their own knowledge to hold them. They ask Allah to hold their hearts, because guidance and going astray are both finally in His hand.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Our Lord! Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us"**: do not let our hearts incline away from the guidance after You let them acquire it. The petition carries a fear inside it, that a heart might slip toward the kind of reading the last verse condemned, trying to interpret the unclear in ways that are not appropriate for us, as happened to the hearts of others.

**"Grant us Your mercy"**: give us mercy from You, ladunka, with which You make our hearts firm and increase our faith and certainty. As a strengthening, it is mercy that steadies the heart rather than knowledge that flatters it.

**"You are indeed the Giver ˹of all bounties˺"**: You alone are the Bestower. This has also been explained as the Bestower of prophethood and Islam to Muhammad ﷺ, and more simply as the One who gave to the believers before us.

### Why the grounded in knowledge pray this prayer

The earlier verse says that the grounded were not proud of their excellence. This verse adds another of their marks: they pray for steadfastness on the right path, and they pray for it with salvation in the next life in view, not for any worldly gain. That choice teaches something. Whether a heart is led or left belongs to Allah alone. A guided heart leans toward goodness, while a heart abandoned to error bends away from straightness. Since His power is absolute and His will effective, anyone anxious to remain steady goes directly to Him and begs for firmness.

A hadith states the same dependence in an image: "There is no heart which is not there in between the two of Allah's fingers. He makes it firm on the truth as long as He wills, and turns it away from the truth when He wills." The practical conclusion is not despair. It is prayer.

### The prayer the Prophet ﷺ kept on his tongue

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr recorded that Umm Salamah said the Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate, "O You Who changes the hearts, make my heart firm on Your religion", and then recite, "Our Lord! Let not our hearts deviate (from the truth) after You have guided us" (3:8). In another wording the prayer runs, "O reverser of hearts, make our hearts firm on the faith chosen by You." He did not trust even his own standing to an untended heart. He asked for firmness, and he went on asking for it.

### The right posture before the unclear part of the Book

The correct academic and intellectual stand toward the allegorical part of the Qur'an is for a person to admit his limits. He should be content with an abstract understanding of things that cannot be grasped by the senses exactly. When even the mind cannot hold a reality whole, the practical course is not to force a precise meaning, but to pray for protection from drowning in fruitless discussion. He should pray to Allah for the wisdom that lets him recognise his place and rest his faith in those realities without knowing all their details. A Day is coming when they will come into full view, but that cannot happen while a person is still under test in this life. The intellect's path can be slippery. From one angle reality is assessed properly, and from another it is misunderstood. Greater wisdom means learning which angle to trust.

### What this supplication means when it is answered

When these people were truthful in asking for help, Allah assisted them with the lights of sufficiency. When the heart is limpid, the present moment is empty, and the tongue is flowing with the remembrance of the Real, the arrow of supplication inevitably reaches the target of response. The hard part is the coming together of that limpidity, loyalty and supplication. The sense of their words is, "O God, keep our hearts far from confusion and straying and make us firm on the carpet of service with the stipulation of the Sunnah."

"Give us mercy from Thee" asks for a gift rather than wages. Human obedience cannot purchase the Presence of His Majesty, so deeds should be forgotten and bounty awaited. A pīr of the Ṭarīqah said that travellers and obedient servants burst with fear at the words "We shall advance upon what deeds they have done and make them scattered dust" (25:23), yet he called that verse the sweetest in the Qur'an. Asked why, he explained that release from displeasing and unworthy obedience lets the heart cling wholly to grace and mercy.

### In short

- Knowledge does not secure the heart. The grounded in knowledge pray not to deviate after being guided, and they pray for mercy, not for rewards in this world.
- Guidance and straying are in Allah's hand, so steadfastness is asked for from Him, as the Prophet ﷺ asked when he prayed for a firm heart.
- Before the unclear part of the Book the sane posture is humility: believe, do not force a meaning, and wait for the Day when these realities come into view.

9.text:
The ninth verse completes the prayer: "Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day—about which there is no doubt. Surely Allah does not break His promise." The grounded in knowledge pray with the end of time in front of them. They ask not to deviate now because they know they will be gathered then, judged by what they did, and answered for what they disputed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Our Lord! You will certainly gather all humanity for the ˹promised˺ Day"**: You will gather Your creation together on the Day of Return, after they die, to judge between them and decide over what they disputed. That day gathers resurrection following death, an audit of deeds, the Bridge over Hell, the Scale, the Garden and the Fire.

**"about which there is no doubt"**: the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will requite people for their deeds as He promised. There is no uncertainty in it.

**"Surely Allah does not break His promise"**: He never misses the appointed promise of raising the dead. There is a shift of address in these last words, from the second person to the third, and they may also be read as Allah's own speech confirming what His servants say. All people are going to be called back to Him, to be held to account on that Day, and He does not break promises.

### Why this prayer is made in this form

The purpose of shaping the supplication this way is to show where its makers' concern sits. Their concern is with the matter of the Hereafter. That is why they ask for adherence to the path of guidance, and they ask for it so that they may reach its reward. A person who settles the gathering in his mind reads the verses about guidance and error differently, because the reading itself will be answered for.

The same fear sits behind two reports that speak of the earlier verse. ʿĀʾishah reported, in a hadith recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, that the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse of the clear and the unclear and said, "When you see those pursuing the allegorical parts know that these are the ones God refers to in this verse so beware of them." And in al-Kabīr, aṭ-Ṭabarānī transmits that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī heard the Prophet ﷺ say, "I fear nothing for my community except three faults", among them the day the Book would be opened in front of a believer who desires to interpret it, though none knows its interpretation except God, while those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it, all is from our Lord." A short hadith with the same warning, reported at Q. 37 in the chain of that report, is left without a number here because the reference in the material is damaged.

### Today's gathering and tomorrow's

There is a gathering already happening and another still to come. Tomorrow everyone gathers where reward, thawāb, and punishment, ʿiqāb, will be assigned. Today the lovers already gather at approach, iqtirāb. Inner selves, asrār, meet now for the unveiling of Majesty, jalāl, and Beauty, jamāl. Bodies, abshār, will meet later amid the terrors, ahwāl, and the states, aḥwāl, foretold for them. The prayer of this verse belongs to people who live in the first gathering with their eyes on the second.

Allah will reward or punish each person according to the deeds he did in this life. That is the whole burden of the verse, and it is the reason the grounded in knowledge say their earlier words at all. They believe, they refuse to chase what can only be settled at the gathering, and they ask to be held to the path until they reach it.

### In short

- All humanity will be gathered on a Day with no doubt in it, and Allah does not break His promise.
- On that Day disputes are decided and every person is rewarded or punished for what he did here.
- The prayer names the gathering in order to fix concern on the Hereafter, since that concern is what makes a reader hold to the path now.

10.text:
The tenth verse turns from prayer to threat: "Indeed, neither the wealth nor children of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah—and they will be the fuel for the Fire". Wealth and children are the two things people most often trust to stand between them and harm. For the disbelievers neither will avail, and they themselves will be fed to the Fire.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, neither the wealth nor children of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah"**: on the Day of Resurrection, what they were granted in this life will not avail them with Allah or save them from His punishment or severe torment. The disbelievers meant are those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, denied His messengers, defied His Books and took no benefit from His revelation to His prophets. In this context the verse was read of Kaʿb Ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and also of Abū Jahl and his companions, people rich in possessions and rich in children.

**"and they will be the fuel for the Fire"**: they are the wood with which the Fire is kindled and fed, the firewood of Hell. Their wealth and children will not protect them from Allah's punishment in this world or in the Afterlife, and they themselves will be the fuel with which Hell is lit on the Day of Resurrection.

### What the Qur'an says elsewhere about this wealth

Allah sets the same emptiness out in several places. "The Day when their excuses will be of no profit to wrongdoers. Theirs will be the curse, and theirs will be the evil abode (i.e. painful torment in Hell-fire)" (40:52). The wealth and children that impress onlookers are themselves part of the punishment: "So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world, and that their souls shall depart (die) while they are disbelievers" (9:55). Nor should the free disposal and affluence of the disbelievers across the land deceive anyone: "Let not the free disposal (and affluence) of the disbelievers throughout the land deceive you. A brief enjoyment; then, their ultimate abode is Hell; and worst indeed is that place for rest" (3:196-197). And the fire they go to is fed by more than their bodies: "Certainly you (disbelievers) and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah, are (but) fuel for Hell!" (21:98).

### A warning that carries a kindness inside it

There is a gentleness hidden in the threat, for the God who warns unbelievers in these words is majestic, generous and lovingly kind. He promises the faithful in the very middle of warning the unbelievers, and He caresses some while blaming others. His point stands in two directions. At the resurrection unbelievers gain nothing from property or offspring. Believers, by contrast, may benefit when dues are paid, religion is held firmly through what they own, and endless happiness is sought by means of it.

Muṣṭafā ﷺ said, "How excellent are wholesome possessions for the wholesome man! What excellent assistance are possessions for being wary of God!" And the Lord of the Worlds says, "And, with what God has given thee..." (28:77), calling a person to bring the next world to hand with what this world has given him, and to seek the felicity of the next world through it. Begin at the table. Food, drink and clothing strengthen the soul. A strengthened soul performs bodily obedience. Obedience supplies the lamp's material while divine bestowal is the lamp's root. The lamp of tawḥīd lights the heart, and a lit heart recognizes God, where the felicity of the next world lies. Possessions, traced backward through those steps, can therefore serve endless happiness.

### The measure that keeps wealth from turning against its owner

The steps only work up to a measure. A person must not pass beyond the measure of sufficiency, because then possessions turn into a cause of rebellion, as He says: "No indeed; surely man is rebellious because..." (96:6-7). That is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked, "Lord God, make the food of Muhammad's family in the measure of sufficiency!" When sufficiency frees time for worship, it shares worship's worth, because provisions for a journey belong to the journey itself. A lawful landed estate supplied Shaykh Abū'l-Qāsim al-Kurragānī with the sufficiency he lived on.

### In short

- Wealth and children will not avail disbelievers against Allah, and the disbelievers themselves will be the fuel of the Fire.
- The same wealth that amazes people in this world is, for those who reject, a brief enjoyment that ends in Hell.
- For the faithful, wealth handled rightly and kept to the measure of sufficiency becomes road-supplies toward recognition of God, whose root is the lamp of tawḥīd.

11.text:
The eleventh verse sets the present disbelievers inside an old pattern: "Their fate will be like that of the people of Pharaoh and those before them—they all rejected Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment". Nothing new is being invented for them. The same conduct met the same end before, and their wealth and children will no more save them than it saved anyone earlier.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Their fate will be like that of the people of Pharaoh and those before them"**: their case is like the case of the people of Pharaoh and of those before them who disbelieved in Allah and denied His signs. The word translated "fate" here is daʾb, which means a people's practice, behaviour, tradition and habit. Ad-Daḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as "like the behaviour of the people of Firʿawn", and ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Abū Mālik, ad-Daḥḥāk and others read it the same way. Others took it as practice, conduct and likeness, and these meanings are all possible, because the daʾb of a people is the way they habitually behave.

**"they all rejected Our signs"**: those before them rejected the messengers, the verses and the proofs that Allah sent with them. The text's history lesson is short. His own people lied to Muhammad ﷺ and mistreated him, just as Moses' people lied to Mūsā (Moses) and mistreated him.

**"so Allah seized them for their sins"**: He seized and destroyed them on account of their denial. The earlier end has a present tense inside it. Allah says to His Messenger that He will do with these people on the day of Badr what He did with the people of Moses on the day of the drowning, and that seizure, like the drowning, will be for the sin of disbelieving the Scripture and the Messenger sent to them.

**"And Allah is severe in punishment"**: His punishment is severe and His torment is painful, when He does punish. Nothing escapes His grasp and nothing escapes His knowledge. He does what He wills and prevails over all things. Everything is humbled before Him, and there is no deity worthy of worship and no Lord except Him.

### The peoples named as parallels

Pharaoh's folk stand first, and after them the communities that came before, such as ʿĀd and Thamūd, who denied the signs of Allah. The verse compresses them into one picture: signs offered and refused, a prophet given the lie and mistreated, and then seizure. The sense of the warning is that this is the end the disbelievers of this generation will meet, and that neither wealth nor children changes the result, just as neither saved the peoples before them.

### Why defeat is a pattern, not an accident

An inward reading hears two ways persisting side by side. They kept to insolence as their sunna, and Allah answered with retribution as His sunna. They refused to abandon persistence and never aspired to good, wa-lā fī l-mabārri Ṭamiʿū. Regret and distress overtook them for what they sent ahead, only to find the door shut, wajadū l-bāba masdūdan, and their regret turned back on them, wa-l-nadama ʿalayhim mardūdan. The door they found shut was the one they had refused to enter while it stood open.

### In short

- These disbelievers repeat the daʾb, the settled behaviour, of Pharaoh's people and those before them, from ʿĀd and Thamūd onward: the lie given to prophets, and then seizure for sin.
- Their wealth and children will avail them no more than it availed those nations, and Badr is named as the drowning's counterpart.
- Allah is severe in punishment, and nothing escapes His grasp or His knowledge.

12.text:
The Prophet ﷺ is told to say to the disbelievers: "Soon you will be overpowered and driven to Hell—what an evil place to rest!" The defeat is placed in this world and the gathering in the next. The words were heard after Badr by people who still thought that the result in the field said nothing about who was right.

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹O Prophet!˺ Tell the disbelievers"**: the warning is given as a direct address. The disbelievers named in the reports that follow are the Jews of Madinah after Badr, and the command runs without restriction as to religion: believers will defeat them and Allah will gather them in the fire of Hell.

**"Soon you will be overpowered"**: you will be defeated in this life. The word can be read as sa-tughlabūn, "you shall be vanquished", or sa-yughlabūn, "they shall be vanquished". For the people addressed the defeat came through killing, capture, imprisonment, the paying of jizya and expulsion.

**"and driven to Hell"**: gathered together on the Day of Resurrection to Hell. Here too the reading runs in two forms, wa-tuḥsharūna, "you will be mustered", or wa-yuhsharūna, "they will be mustered". The mustering is in the Hereafter, and the place they enter is the fire.

**"what an evil place to rest!"**: an evil cradling and an evil resting place, an evil place and outcome.

### The objection raised by the Jews of Madinah after Badr

ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatādah related that, after victory at Badr, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Al-Madinah and summoned the Jews at the market of Banū Qaynuqāʿ. Muḥammad ibn Ishaq bin Yasar preserves the report. The Prophet ﷺ warned them not to let Badr's fate reach them as it had reached Quraysh, and he called them into Islam beforehand. He added that prophethood was no secret to them, since their Scripture and Allah's covenant both mentioned him.

Their reply rejected the warning. Quraysh, they said, were inexperienced men ignorant of warfare, so let him not be deluded by beating them. If Jews fought, he would discover real fighters. This verse followed. ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr transmit the account from Ibn ʿAbbās, and a shorter version records the same taunt after the Prophet ﷺ urged the Jews to accept Islam on his return.

### A second report about the Jews of Madinah

Ibn ʿAbbās also reports a change after Uhud. At Badr the Jews of Medina had identified Muhammad ﷺ as the unlettered Prophet announced by Moses, whose description stood in their Scriptures and whose banner would never fall. Some wanted immediate faith, while others counselled waiting for another encounter. Defeat at Uhud reversed them. They denied that he could be the promised prophet, abandoned Islam, and broke a treaty that still had time to run. Then Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf rode toward Mecca with sixty riders, met Abū Sufyān's party, agreed on one common word and purpose, and returned to Medina. Revelation answered them in this verse.

### To which disbelievers does the promise apply?

The warning does not claim that every unbeliever everywhere loses in this world. Its horizon is the generation addressed. Pagans among them fell in battle or were captured. Jews were subdued through deaths, captivity, expulsion and jizya. Doubt dissolves when the promise is confined to those hearers and the fate they actually met.

### The pain they already carry without knowing it

The Real's speech will pass them by later, in ājil, and even now, in the present or ʿājil, living holds no delight for them. Tomorrow brings burning punishment, ḥurqa. Today already brings furqa, absence and separation from God, but dim insight cannot feel the pain of a punishment already begun.

### In short

- The disbelievers addressed after Badr are told they will be overpowered in this world and gathered to Hell in the next.
- The Jews of Madinah answered the call to Islam by calling the Quraysh inexperienced, and after Uhud some broke their treaty and rode with Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf to Abū Sufyān.
- The overcoming named here belongs to the disbelievers of that time, beaten by killing, capture, jizya and expulsion, and not to every disbeliever in every age.

13.text:
This verse, "Indeed, there was a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle—one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial. The believers saw their enemy twice their number. But Allah supports with His victory whoever He wills. Surely in this is a lesson for people of insight", looks back to Badr as proof of the warning in the verse before it. A small force with very little equipment defeated a force about three times its size, and the seeing of the two armies was itself part of the sign.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, there was a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle"**: this āyah proves that Allah exalts His religion, grants success to His Messenger, makes His word visible and raises faith above rivals. For the Jews addressed, Badr also confirms Muhammad's prophethood. Two camps met there in combat.

**"one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial"**: one camp fought in the cause of Allah, the Muslims. The other fought in disbelief, the idolaters of Quraysh at Badr. The first group fought in obedience to Allah, Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions. The second consisted of disbelievers in Allah and His Messenger, Abū Sufyān and his army, who had come out of Makkah in pride and for show.

**"The believers saw their enemy twice their number"**: the two sides did not see the numbers in the same way, and the material explains the sighting in more than one way. These explanations are set out in the section on the double sighting below.

**"But Allah supports with His victory whoever He wills"**: help is His to assign. He strengthened the side He chose and stood by His allies, and He grants believing servants success now and again on the Day when witnesses rise.

**"Surely in this is a lesson for people of insight"**: a lesson for those who understand, people of vision who are discerning. They should think about Allah's wisdom, decisions and decree. The lesson is also put as a question to the hearers: after this, will you not be warned, and believe?

### The numbers at Badr

The imbalance began with people and animals: Quraysh fielded about 1000 men. Their animals included 700 camels plus 100 horses. Opposing them stood just over 300 Muslims. Muslims brought only 2 horses, carried 8 swords and 6 armours, and shared 70 camels. A precise count sets Muhammad's men at 313, mostly foot soldiers, while Abū Sufyān commanded 950. A tiny, poorly supplied force had nevertheless overturned a much larger one, exactly as promised earlier at Makkah. Observers willing to learn could hardly miss the event.

In the fourteenth year of prophethood Badr supplied this world with an image of the next. Deniers held every advantage of manpower and might, whereas believers possessed almost no worldly power. Yet denial collapsed and faith prevailed decisively. Without divine succour, such reversal across so large a resource gap is impossible. Truth therefore never stands unsupported, and Allah sides with believers. For deniers, the event exposes their real position. They had evidence in the preacher's speech and conduct, but pride sheltered behind elegant rebuttals and invented explanations. Death eventually removes that shelter, and the next world shows those arguments to be empty.

### The double sighting: who saw whom as twice?

The verse's own wording allows two sightings, and both are reported. In one reading, the idolaters thought the Muslims were twice as many as they really were, and Allah made that illusion one of the factors in the victory of Islam over them. In the other, the Muslims saw twice as many idolators as themselves, and Allah still gave them victory over the disbelievers.

ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd said, "When we looked at the disbelievers' forces, we found that they were twice as many as we were. When we looked at them again, we thought they did not have one man more than we had." His words stand beside the verse in al-Anfal: "And (remember) when you met, He showed them to you as few in your eyes and He made you appear as few in their eyes" (8:44).

Timing separates the sightings. At first sight, Muslims estimated their opponents at double their actual strength, which drove them toward trust and prayer for help. Quraysh made the mirror error about believers, and terror followed. Believers also clung to another promise: "If there be among you a hundred patient one, they shall over-come two hundred" (8:66). Had the true ratio (roughly three to one) registered, fear might have overwhelmed them. Once ranks closed, perception reversed again. Each army appeared small to the other, daring both to engage, "so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained" (8:42). That ordained result separated truth from falsehood, lifted faith over unbelief, and humiliated the deniers. Allah names the outcome himself: "And Allah has already made you victorious at Badr, when you were a weak little force" (3:123).

Jewish onlookers receive a second application. They personally watched unbelievers outnumber Muhammad's Companions twofold, yet Allah still delivered triumph at Badr. Because they never fought, the bare outcome carries the proof.

### Inner sight and outer sight

An inward reading notices perception itself being governed. To finish an affair, Allah can enlarge a few in one people's eyes and shrink a multitude in another's. Cover the inner eye, baṣīra, and keen outer eyes, abṣār, profit nothing. Open the inmost self, and obstructed insight, baṣāʾir, cannot hurt. Armies thought they were reporting numbers, but seeing had already been arranged by the One arranging victory.

### In short

- At Badr about 313 Muslims with 70 camels, 2 horses, 6 armours and 8 swords defeated some 950 to 1000 Quraysh, and that result is the sign.
- Each army saw the other as twice its number at one moment, and as few at another, so that both would fight and the ordained outcome would become clear (8:42, 8:44, 8:66, 3:123).
- The lesson is for people of insight: victory comes from Allah's support, not from numbers, and outer eyes are useless when inner sight is covered.

14.text:
Desire for worldly things, the verse says, "has been made appealing to people". The list runs "The enjoyment of ˹worldly˺ desires—women, children, treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle, and fertile land—has been made appealing to people. These are the pleasures of this worldly life, but with Allah is the finest destination." The verse does not call these things evil. It calls them enjoyable, temporary, and dangerous when they occupy the heart, because hostility to truth usually grows out of love for them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The enjoyment of ˹worldly˺ desires—women, children, treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle, and fertile land—has been made appealing to people"**: what the self wants and calls for has been beautified. Women are named first because the test through them is more tempting, then children, because most earning is done for a wife and children to share. After them come stored and piled wealth in gold and silver, the qanāṭir al-muqanṭarah, then fine marked horses, livestock and tilled land. For unbelievers these things are made attractive in a special way, while for everyone they form the working material of life.

**"These are the pleasures of this worldly life"**: they give benefit for a while and then vanish. One explanation likens their duration to the useful life of household things, a bowl or a plate, after which the object is gone.

**"but with Allah is the finest destination"**: the more excellent abode and best return is with Him, Paradise in the Hereafter. A believer should desire no other final home, and should not become attached to gifts whose best use is to lead there.

### Women, children, wealth and horses: how each desire can turn

It is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I did not leave behind me a test more tempting to men than women." Yet attraction is not condemned in itself. When a man enjoys marriage in order to preserve chastity and have children, he is encouraged. Marriage is urged in many hadiths, including the words that the best members of this ummah are those with the most wives. Another hadith calls this life a delight and its best delight a righteous wife. The Prophet ﷺ also said that women and perfume were made dear to him, while the comfort of his eye was prayer. ʿĀʾishah reported his dearest worldly love as women, with horses next in one version and before them in another.

Children likewise divide by intention. Desire for children can become pride and boasting, and then it tempts. When the aim is to increase the ummah of Muhammad ﷺ with worshippers of Allah alone, it is praised. A hadith says, "Marry the Wadud (kind) and Walud (fertile) woman, for I will compare your numbers to the rest of the nations on the Day of Resurrection."

Wealth divides in the same way. Wanting money can grow from arrogance, the wish to dominate the weak and control the poor, and that is forbidden. It can also be sought for worship, kindness to family and relatives, and spending in righteousness and obedience, and then it is praised. Scholars disagreed over the amount of a qinṭār, though Ad-Daḥḥāk and others all make it a large sum of money. Abū Hurayrah put it as twelve thousand ūqiyah, adding that each ūqiyah is better than what lies between heaven and earth. Ibn Jarīr recorded that report.

Horses fall into three classes. Some are collected for the cause of Allah and used in battle when needed, and their owner is rewarded. Some are kept for boasting and hostility toward the people of Islam, and their owner earns a burden. Some are kept for need and breeding while Allah's right over them is not forgotten, and they become a shield of sufficiency for their owner. The same threefold division stands behind the command, "And make ready against them all you can of power, including steeds of war" (8:60). The musawwamah horses drew two explanations. Makḥūl pointed to a horse marked by a white-spotted face and white feet. Ibn ʿAbbās called them branded, beautiful animals, and the same account came from Abū Sinān, as-Suddī, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn Abzā, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid. Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Dharr heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that every Arabian horse is allowed two supplications each dawn, asking Allah, who made it subservient to the son of Adam, to make it among the dearest of his wealth and household, or the dearest of his household and wealth, to him.

Cattle means camels, cows and sheep. Fertile land means land used to farm and grow plants. None of these is dismissed. Each is measured by the use to which it is put.

### Why attraction was built into human beings

Jihad against hostile disbelievers occupied the verses before this, and now the text explains why people make themselves hostile. Love of the world is called the head of error, and the people ranged against truth are driven by wealth, power, lust or defence of ancestral custom. All are reaching for a share of present enjoyment.

There is wisdom in the attraction itself. If people had no natural inclination toward family, food, trade and land, worldly business would collapse. Nobody would sweat over farms and fields, work for wages, risk capital in industry, stock a shop, or go out to buy what is needed to live. Love of desirable things draws workers, employers, traders and customers out of their houses and silently keeps a social system running. There is a second wisdom. A person who had no taste for blessings here would have no appetite for blessings promised in the next world, and no motive to do good and avoid evil. And there is a third, more searching wisdom. Attraction sets the test. One person becomes engrossed in present enjoyment and forgets the life to come. Another sees these things as real but temporary, takes what he needs, and directs his effort toward making the next life good and safe. Allah states the testing purpose in His words: "We made whatever there is on the earth its adornment so that We can test as to who among them acts best" (18:7).

Where other verses say that Satan made deeds look attractive (8:48) (16:63) (27:24) (29:38), the attraction belongs to things evil in religion and reason, or to enjoyment pushed past Allah's limits. Lawful adornment is not bad in itself. That is why the placing of attraction in things is elsewhere attributed to Allah.

### The boat, and the water around it

The practical rule is moderation. Good things may be sought and stored according to genuine need. Using them in forbidden ways, or indulging until the reality after death is forgotten, is self-destruction. The poet-sage Rūmī pictured the heart as a boat and worldly things as water. Water beneath and around a boat supports it and serves its purpose. Water inside the boat capsizes it and destroys everything in it. Wealth and possessions are meant to stay underneath a person, carrying him in this world and toward the next, not to enter the heart and kill it.

That distinction changes the value of the same possessions. One person enjoys present blessings and uses them as milestones toward a prosperous Hereafter, so they never become a roadblock. Another squanders his chance at the next life through them, and they begin to punish him already here: "So, their wealth and children should not attract you. Allah wants to punish them with these in this lowly life" (9:55). This world is a place of trial. Worldly acquisitions bring social honour, and family, wealth and property become the centre of interest until no future beyond this life is remembered, no other home is considered, and no other wealth seems worth a life's devotion. Only a person whose focus rests on the permanent life sees how small these glittering things are in the scale of the unseen.

### Paradise ringed by hardship

Muṣṭafā ﷺ, the world's paragon and master of Adam's children, told that the Eternal Enactor first created Paradise and sent Gabriel to inspect what awaited His servants and friends. Gabriel returned from gardens of endless bliss near Allah's Presence and swore that nobody hearing their description would fail to strive and obey. Only then did God ring Paradise with hardship, disappointment, unworthy distractions and desires left unmet, placing a bridge of trial across its road for every seeker of the Patron.

Shaykh al-Islām Anṣārī wondered at hidden reversals: disappointment can conceal a thousand treasures, suffering can mother happiness, union's exaltation can hide inside bewilderment's abasement, and companionship can amount to the greatest Resurrection. The Kaʿbah remains sweet as God's friends nest there truthfully, yet a man-eating desert stretches before it through mile and station after station. Who finally seeks hard enough to cross?
